sections.h2: Does Tennessee tax the profit when I sell a house?
sections.html:
Tennessee does not charge a state tax on the profit from a home sale. The Department of Revenue describes its old Hall income tax as a levy only on interest from bonds and notes and dividends from stock, and that tax was repealed for tax periods beginning January 1, 2021 or later. The Department's help desk adds that Tennessee has no individual income tax on wages, employer sponsored retirement income or most other forms of income.

That leaves the federal return as the place where a Tennessee seller reports a gain. If a business entity, rather than a person, owns the house, ask the Department of Revenue how that entity is treated before you set a closing date.

sections.h2: How much of the gain can a Tennessee homeowner exclude on the federal return?
sections.html:
A seller can exclude up to $250,000 of gain on a main home, or up to $500,000 on a joint return, if both the ownership and use tests are met. The IRS explains in Topic no. 701 that you must have owned the home for at least 24 months and used it as a residence for at least 24 months during the five years before the sale. The two periods do not have to be the same 24 months.

  • On a joint return, either spouse can satisfy the ownership test, but both spouses must meet the use test.
  • The exclusion is generally unavailable if you excluded the gain on another home during the two years before this sale.
  • Service members and certain Foreign Service and intelligence community employees on qualified extended duty can elect to suspend the five year test period for up to 10 years.

Publication 523 holds the full eligibility rules and the worksheets. Pull it before you decide whether a Tennessee sale produces any taxable gain at all.

sections.h2: Do I have to report a Tennessee home sale if the gain is excluded?
sections.html:
Yes, in one situation. If you receive a Form 1099-S, Proceeds From Real Estate Transactions, the IRS says you must report the sale even when every dollar of gain is excludable. You must also report it when part of the gain exceeds the exclusion.

When reporting is required, the sale goes on Form 8949 and then Schedule D of Form 1040. Keep the closing disclosure, your purchase paperwork and receipts for improvements, because the IRS defines basis as generally what you paid plus the cost of improvements that add value. A Tennessee seller who bought a house years ago and finished a kitchen or added a deck can subtract those costs from the sale price when figuring the gain.

sections.h2: What federal rates apply to gain above the exclusion?
sections.html:
Gain on a home held more than one year is a long-term gain, and the IRS says most net capital gain is taxed at no more than 15 percent for most individuals. The brackets below come from IRS Topic no. 409 for taxable years beginning in 2025, so check the IRS page for the thresholds that apply to your sale year.

Filing status0% rate up to taxable income of15% rate up to taxable income of
Single$48,350$533,400
Married filing jointly$96,700$600,050
Head of household$64,750$566,700
Married filing separately$48,350$300,000

Taxable income above the 15 percent ceiling is taxed at 20 percent. A gain on a house held one year or less is short-term and taxed as ordinary income.

sections.h2: How is an inherited Tennessee house taxed when the heirs sell it?
sections.html:
An heir's starting figure is usually the market value on the date of death, not what the decedent paid. IRS Publication 551 says the basis of inherited property is generally the fair market value at the date of death, or the value on the alternate valuation date if the executor chose it. Heirs who sell soon after receiving the property often owe little or no federal tax, because the sale price sits close to that stepped-up value.

  • If the estate filed a federal estate tax return, beneficiaries generally receive a Schedule A (Form 8971) showing the value to use as basis.
  • If no Schedule A arrives, Publication 551 says the appraised value at the date of death for state inheritance or transmission tax purposes can be used.
  • A house you gave to a person who then left it back to you within one year of their death keeps the original owner's basis instead of the date-of-death value.

Get a date-of-death appraisal before listing. It protects the basis you will report on Schedule D.

sections.h2: What Tennessee tax is due at closing when the house sells?
sections.html:
The state charge on a sale is the realty transfer tax, part of the recordation tax. The Department of Revenue lists the rate at $0.37 per $100 of purchase price, so a $300,000 sale carries $1,110. The county register of deeds collects it and sends it to the Department, which states that the grantee, the person receiving the deed, pays the realty transfer tax to the register.

A mortgage the buyer takes out brings a separate mortgage tax of $0.115 per $100 of debt, with the first $2,000 exempt. That one belongs to the borrower. Ask the register of deeds in your county how the office wants the transfer tax figure documented on the deed.

sections.h2: What if I take payments over several years or turn the house into a rental first?
sections.html:
Both choices change how the gain is reported. IRS Topic no. 705 says a sale with at least one payment after the year of sale is an installment sale, reported on Form 6252 under the installment method unless you elect out. Only the part of each payment that exceeds your basis counts as income that year, and interest is ordinary income.

Renting the house first adds depreciation. Publication 551 sets the depreciation basis at the lesser of the market value on the date of the change or your adjusted basis. Topic no. 409 also notes that unrecaptured section 1250 gain from real property is taxed at a maximum 25 percent rate. A Tennessee landlord selling a former home should ask a tax preparer to run the numbers before accepting an offer.

sections.h2: Which official pages should a Tennessee seller check?
sections.html:
Start with the Tennessee Department of Revenue for state questions, the IRS for the exclusion and rates, and your county register of deeds for the recording steps. The IRS pages above carry their own update dates, and tax figures change each year.

  • IRS Topic no. 701 and Publication 523 for the exclusion and worksheets.
  • IRS Topic no. 409 for the rate brackets and where to report.
  • IRS Publication 551 for inherited and gifted property basis.
  • Tennessee Department of Revenue recordation tax pages for the transfer tax.

faqs.q: Is there a Tennessee capital gains tax on a house?
faqs.a: No. Tennessee has no individual income tax on wages or most other income, and the Hall tax on interest and dividends was repealed for periods beginning January 1, 2021 or later. Your federal return still applies to any gain above the exclusion.

faqs.q: What is the federal home sale exclusion?
faqs.a: It is $250,000 of gain for a single seller or $500,000 on a joint return. You need 24 months of ownership and 24 months of use as a main home within the five years before the sale.

faqs.q: Do heirs pay tax on a house they inherit and sell?
faqs.a: They pay federal tax only on gain measured from the stepped-up value, which is generally the market value at the date of death. A sale near that value often produces little gain. Keep a date-of-death appraisal.

faqs.q: How much is the Tennessee realty transfer tax?
faqs.a: It is $0.37 per $100 of purchase price, according to the Department of Revenue. The grantee pays it to the county register of deeds when the deed is recorded.

faqs.q: Do I report the sale if the gain is under the exclusion?
faqs.a: Only if you got a Form 1099-S or part of the gain is taxable. When you do report, use Form 8949 and Schedule D. A seller with no 1099-S and a fully excluded gain generally has nothing to report.
